| [NOTE-265](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-265.md) | What Happens When Someone Acts? | Velleman argues that the "standard story" of action (desire + belief cause an intention, which causes movement) leaves the agent out. It fails even when every causal link is normal: his example is an intention to end a friendship, formed and executed without him (p. 104). Frankfurt's hierarchical remedy cannot fix it either. Any mental item picked out without presupposing the agent's participation (a second-order desire, a Watsonian value, a "decisive commitment") is one the agent can be alienated from. Any item defined so as to guarantee participation begs the question of agent-causation (pp. 112–116). His alternative is to look for what is *functionally identical* to the agent, not what the agent identifies with. That can only be a motive always behind and never merely in front of critical reflection: the desire to act in accordance with reasons. Its reinforcing force is the agent's contribution (pp. 117–122). | Read |

| [NOTE-267](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-267.md) | Personal Autonomy | The entry sorts accounts of self-government into four families: "coherentist" (hierarchical desires, Frankfurt; evaluative judgments, Watson; plans, Bratman; caring; character), reasons-responsive, responsiveness-to-reasoning (Christman, Mele) and incompatibilist, with relational conditions as a compatible add-on. | [NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md) | Identification and Identity | Velleman targets Frankfurt's *later* conception of autonomy. On that conception, a person acts autonomously only when his volitions derive from "the essential character of his will", and that essence consists of volitional necessities that are also the conditions of his personal identity. Velleman argues against it on three grounds. Such an essence would ground authenticity, not autonomy (the Winnicottian False Self is inauthentic but over-controlled). Frankfurt offers no argument or example that motivational change ends a person. And the ideal of wholeheartedness, which cures ambivalence by extruding a desire from the self, is a defensive fantasy: Freud's Rat Man was made ill by just such a separation, and identifying with part of oneself in the ordinary, imaginative sense is Sartrean bad faith. He replaces "the self" with an *aspectual* reading of "self" as a marker of reflexivity. On that reading autonomy is behaviour motivated partly by the understanding, the part of us "with which we cannot help identifying", without its being our identity (pp. 357–360). | Read |
| [NOTE-269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-269.md) | Moral Responsibility and the Principle of Alternative Possibilities | PAP ("a person is morally responsible for what she has done only if she could have done otherwise") has no decisive positive argument: it is not self-evident, and the moral arguments from fairness, OIC and the W-defense cover blame at most. Frankfurt-style cases (FSCs) are the strongest attack, because the factor that makes the act inevitable plays no role in producing it. The entry lays out three defences of PAP: - general-ability readings (PAP-general); - "flickers of freedom", which Fischer answers with the robustness requirement; - the Kane/Widerker/Ginet dilemma, answered by Fischer's causal-irrelevance reply on the first horn and by Pereboom's buffer case, Hunt's blockage and Mele & Robb 1998 on the second. Robb reports "not much consensus" (§5). He treats the fall of PAP as re-energising compatibilism, with Frankfurt's 1971 identification view and Fischer & Ravizza's guidance control as the two replacement accounts. | Read |
| [NOTE-270](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-270.md) | Compatibilism | The entry sorts compatibilism by which incompatibilist premise it denies: that free will requires the ability to do otherwise, that determinism precludes it, or that free will requires ultimate sourcehood. It argues that every "mesh" compatibilism has the same weak point: its sufficient conditions (hierarchies, reasons-responsive mechanisms, values) can be installed by manipulation, so each must either show what is wrong with manipulation cases or accept them. Its §4.2.1 is the fullest statement of Frankfurt 1971 in this batch. The current revision has **dropped the wanton/person distinction**. The 2004–2015 revisions had it ("passive bystanders to their wills", 1971, p. 89) and have to be read for it. | Read |
| [NOTE-339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-339.md) | Examining the Society of Mind | An exposition, read in full. Singh dates the Society of Mind to Minsky and Papert's early-1970s robot work, finds its agent in the procedure-bearing frame of 1974, and quotes the unpublished 1976 book drafts. | [NOTE-341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-341.md) | The Computational Boundary of a "Self" | A hypothesis essay. A Self is the set of parts that pursue goals together, and its boundary is the farthest region of space and time it can measure and act on, its "cognitive light cone". Selves grow from homeostatic loops by adding memory, anticipation and networks, and cells form larger Selves by sharing bioelectric state through gap junctions. | [NOTE-345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-345.md) | Chalmers — Could a large language model be conscious? | Asks for a feature X that indicates LLM consciousness or its absence. Six obstacles stand against it: biology, senses and embodiment, world and self models, recurrence, a global workspace and unified agency, the last three strongest, all but biology temporary. | [NOTE-348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-348.md) | The Emotion Machine | Read in the 2005 draft. Emotions are Ways to Think: each emotional state is a selection of mental resources turned on and off, made by Selectors that Critics trigger when they recognise a type of problem, and ordinary thinking uses the same switching. On this design sit six levels of mental activity, panalogies that link descriptions across realms, and a Self that is a network of partial models. | [NOTE-351](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-351.md) | Intelligence without representation | A methodological manifesto with working robots behind it. | [NOTE-353](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-353.md) | True Believers: The Intentional Strategy and Why It Works | Belief is objective but visible only through a strategy: a true believer is any system "reliably and voluminously predictable" by treating it as a rational agent with the beliefs and desires it ought to have. | [NOTE-372](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-372.md) | Self models | Metzinger's compact statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity. Self-models can be unconscious and artificial, and embodiment comes in three orders. The central claim is stated with a prediction, not argued; the examples are cited. | [NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | A short review that sets the minimal self (present self-consciousness) against the narrative self (extended in time), splits the minimal self into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, and ties their dissociation in schizophrenic thought insertion to Frith's forward comparator model. | [NOTE-382](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-382.md) | Shanahan — Simulacra as Conscious Exotica | A Wittgensteinian treatment: consciousness talk is anchored in what is public, so an exotic entity is a candidate only if we could engineer an encounter with it in a shared world. Disembodied chat agents are not candidates; virtually embodied ones could be. On the self: no "self worth preserving" without body, history and autobiographical memory, and no "person behind the mask" for a role player, whose identity is a shifting distribution of roles. | [NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle restates the 1995 theory in twenty pages. Social facts are facts involving collective intentionality. Institutional facts are the subclass in which collective acceptance imposes a status function, "X counts as Y in C", carrying deontic powers that give desire-independent reasons for action. Language is constitutive, since such facts exist only as represented. He revises the book in two places: status indicators matter in their own right, and some Y terms are free-standing, with no X, as with corporations and money without currency. "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is now ranked as the more general form. Collective intentionality is assumed, not argued for. | Read |
| [NOTE-393](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-393.md) | Epstein — Social Ontology (SEP) | A survey organised by its author's own distinction: what grounds a social fact versus what anchors the category it falls under. It reports that ontological individualism is widely assumed and now contested; that grounding has displaced supervenience; that convention, collective acceptance, patterns, practices and language are rival theories of anchoring; and that whether anchoring is a distinct relation is disputed. It covers groups, group agency, institutions, race and gender, artifacts, money, law and language. Survey claims are reported, not argued; one citation (Epstein 2016) is missing from the bibliography, and Schwitzgebel 2015 is listed with critics of group phenomenal states. | Read |
| [NOTE-421](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-421.md) | Life as we know it | The flow of internal and active states in an ergodic system with a Markov blanket, written in Helmholtz form, can be redescribed as gradient descent on a variational free energy once the variational density is set equal to the posterior over external states. On that redescription such systems "appear" to infer and to bound their own entropy, which the paper calls the marks of life. One simulated soup shows a blanket-enclosed cluster that predicts external motion and falls apart under lesions. The free energy is variational, not thermodynamic. The candle flame is excluded by a one-sentence assertion. The paper's own reported p-value is not reproduced by the null it describes. | Read |
| [NOTE-433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-433.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda's action-readiness theory applied to impulsive action. Automatic appraisal of concern pertinence elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change a self–object relation, with control precedence. Emotions differ by mode of action readiness. Events draw several appraisals at once, and the resulting states of readiness interact, so impulse control and much emotion regulation are themselves emotional. Purposive impulsive action is grounded neurally in anticipating an action's sensory effects (PPC, premotor, cerebellum), with frontostriatal circuits for stopping. | Read |
| [NOTE-438](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-438.md) v2 | A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation | 128 experiments on interesting tasks, separate meta-analyses for free-choice behaviour and self-reported interest. Tangible rewards expected for engaging in, completing or doing well at a task undermine free-choice intrinsic motivation (d from −0.28 to −0.40), and less so self-reports; unexpected and task-noncontingent rewards do not; positive feedback enhances, except for children's free choice. The pattern fits cognitive evaluation theory and contradicts Eisenberger and Cameron's helplessness and learned-industriousness account. | Read |
| [NOTE-439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-439.md) | The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior | Needs in SDT are innate psychological nutriments, identified functionally by the costs of their thwarting, not by individual differences in their strength. The three needs organize findings on intrinsic motivation and internalization, predict that both the "why" (autonomous vs controlled regulation) and the "what" (intrinsic vs extrinsic aspirations) of goals affect well-being, and explain need substitutes and rigid defences when needs are thwarted. Autonomy is self-organization, defended as an evolved, domain-general design feature. | Read |
| [NOTE-440](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-440.md) | Basic psychological need theory: Advancements, critical themes, and future directions | The authors set out nine criteria a basic psychological need must meet, separate need frustration from mere lack of satisfaction, review need frustration's costs (ill-being, compensatory behaviour, need substitutes) and propose it as transdiagnostic, review the interplay with sleep, food, sex and safety, map need-supportive and need-thwarting practices on a circumplex, and argue that the needs are universal in their effects ("output side") while the practices that satisfy them vary ("input side"). Novelty, morality and beneficence are weighed as fourth needs and not yet admitted. | Read |
| [NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | SDT's autonomy is "regulation by the self": acting with reflective endorsement, graded along the internalization continuum, compatible with external influence, dependence and a single option. Ryan and Deci align it with phenomenological and hierarchical (Frankfurt, Dworkin) accounts and use that definition to answer behaviourist, social-cognitive, reductionist, nonconscious-priming, choice-overload and cultural critiques. Autonomy lies not in being an uncaused cause but in the capacity to "reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). | Read |
| [NOTE-442](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-442.md) v2 | Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being | SDT's canonical short statement. Social contexts that support competence, autonomy and relatedness sustain intrinsic motivation and let people internalize and integrate extrinsic regulations; controlling, rejecting or overchallenging contexts undermine intrinsic motivation and leave regulations external or introjected. Autonomy is graded: four kinds of extrinsic motivation lie on a continuum of relative autonomy (Ryan & Connell's quasi-simplex). Basic needs are defined by their consequences for well-being, and need-deprivation is offered as a principal source of distress and psychopathology. | Read |
| [NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse with delay alone, so a person is a population of interests that forestall one another. Will is the recursive bundling of choices by treating each as a precedent, which gives an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma and makes Kavka's toxin rational to drink. The same recursion predicts legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control, and premature satiation of appetite limits what will can do for emotional reward. | Read |
| [NOTE-447](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-447.md) | The Emperor's New Markov Blankets | Pearl blankets (conditional-independence shields in a Bayesian network) and Friston blankets (agent–environment boundaries in the world) are different constructs conflated in the free-energy literature. The four-way partition needs a chosen internal node, sensorimotor labels and steady state; in Friston's soup it also needs electrochemical-only coupling and a fixed cluster size. Realist use needs metaphysical premises; instrumental use is innocent but settles nothing about boundaries. | Read |
| [NOTE-452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-452.md) | The Intimate Contest for Self-Command | Schelling's essay proposes "egonomics", the art of managing oneself. Its core claim is that many self-control tactics are the tactics for managing another person, applied to a "sometime self" who will be in command later. It gives a taxonomy of habits by time profile, onset time, warning time, cost, visibility, damage function and self-aggravation. It refuses a general answer to which self is authentic. It estimates the stakes at "on the order of a trillion dollars" for the current population. | Read |
| [NOTE-455](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-455.md) | The Normative Constitution of Agency | Korsgaard asks whether agency is natural (a movement caused by the right mental state) or normatively constituted (a movement backed by an agent whose unity is achieved by following norms). Ordinary attribution of action implies activity and identity. Self-constitution explains both: the categorical and hypothetical imperatives give action the form of self-determined efficacy, and the maxims chosen under them constitute practical identity. Reflective self-consciousness breaks given unity and sets the task of rebuilding it, so unity of agency is "an achievement, not a given". | Read |
| [NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md) | Participatory sense-making: An enactive approach to social cognition | An enactive account of social cognition built on coordination dynamics. When coordination and the encounter shape each other, the interaction gains its own precarious operational closure; it is social only if the interactors stay autonomous. Coordinated sense-making then ranges from one partner's sense-making being modulated to meanings made jointly. Conceptual throughout; evidence is illustrative (corridor, charades, mother–infant timing, perceptual crossing). | Read |
| [NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md) | Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-temporality in Action | Minimal agency needs a self-individuated system that is the source of modulations of its coupling with the environment and regulates them by norms it generates. An autonomous organization, a precarious network of mutually enabling processes, generates all three when it adaptively modulates its coupling for its own maintenance. Life is sufficient, not necessary. The definition is a proposal: the authors say asymmetry's formalization is incomplete and modeller-relative. | Read |
| [NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger's own sketch of the self-model theory. Six constraints (globality, presentationality, transparency, convolved holism, dynamicity, perspectivalness) build up consciousness; a transparent self-model yields phenomenal selfhood, so "no such things as selves exist in the world"; transparency is graded, inversely proportional to the attentional availability of earlier processing stages. Phenomenal unity is one global functional cluster. The first-person perspective is a model of the intentionality relation, whose iteration gives introspective and social intelligence. A theory statement: no new evidence. | Read |
| [NOTE-462](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-462.md) | An Accumulator Model for Spontaneous Neural Activity Prior to Self-Initiated Movement | A three-parameter leaky stochastic accumulator, δx = (I − kx)Δt + cξ√Δt, fitted to Libet-task waiting times (k = 0.5, I = 0.11, threshold at the 80th percentile of output), reproduces the readiness potential (r² = 0.96) and the linear mean–SD relation of waiting times (r = 0.9). In a variant with random clicks, fast responders showed a slow negativity before the click (P < 0.005), and fast and slow clicks were spread equally through the trial (P = 0.64). The neural decision to move is placed at the threshold crossing about 150 ms before movement. | Read |
| [NOTE-464](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-464.md) | A Planning Agent's Self-Governance over Time | Bratman's model of a planning agent's self-governance over time. It needs (1) planned temporally extended activity with a time-frame to "plan's end", (2) synchronic self-governance along the way, (3) cross-temporal links of intention that are intrapersonal analogues of shared intention, so the agent acts "together" with herself, and (4) "diachronicalized" standpoints holding a conditional, reflexive end of diachronic self-governance. The model makes some willpower and resistance to shuffling self-governed and excludes the toxin case. Argued by cases, not tested. | Read |
| [NOTE-465](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-465.md) | The Sources of Normativity | Korsgaard's Tanner Lectures. The normative question (what justifies morality's claims on us) is not answered by voluntarism, substantive realism or reflective endorsement alone. Reflective consciousness forces us to act on reasons, and so to identify with a law: a "practical identity", the description under which we value ourselves. Obligation is the reflective rejection of a threat to that identity. Valuing any identity commits us to valuing humanity, reasons are public, and animals' pain can obligate us. Argued, but "sketchy" by its own account. | Read |
| [NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Persons differ from other creatures in the structure of the will: they have second-order volitions, desires that a given desire be the one that moves them to act, and wantons do not. Forming one is identifying with a desire. Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, and a decisive identification ends the series of higher orders "without cutting it off arbitrarily" (p. 16). Responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts of his own free will. The view is neutral on determinism, and on how the will came to be (n. 10). | Read |
| [NOTE-546](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-546.md) | Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility | Frankfurt argues that PAP is false because circumstances can make an action unavoidable without bringing it about: Black stands ready to make Jones4 act and never needs to, so Jones4 is as responsible, for blame or praise, as he would be without Black (§IV). A fact that explains nothing about the action cannot excuse it (§V). The replacement principle excuses only an agent who acted "only because he could not have done otherwise", and Frankfurt says it is compatible with determinism. | Read |
| [NOTE-547](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-547.md) | Stories and the Meaning of Life | Fischer's own sketch of his framework (guidance control, not regulative control, is the freedom-relevant condition; guidance control is ownership plus moderate reasons-responsiveness; responsibility is historical and compatible with determinism; the Frankfurt cases' moral is the actual sequence), followed by the paper's thesis: acting freely is artistic self-expression that gives a life narrative value, a product judged mainly morally and prudentially, so the activity's aesthetic nature does not fix how the life is evaluated. | Read |
| [NOTE-548](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-548.md) | Moral Responsibility | A survey of moral responsibility. Its most exact reports, for this record: Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control as an owned, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism, with page references (§2.3); Wolf's critique of Real Self views and the requirement that an agent be able to form her values on the basis of the True and the Good (§3.1.1); and the moral competence condition, through JoJo (§3.2). Wolf's praise/blame asymmetry is noted in one sentence. | Read |
| [NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md) | List & Pettit — Group Agency and Supervenience | Four conditions of agency (§2). A group's judgments supervene on members' contributions under a constitution (§3). With a universal domain, robust group rationality is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience (Propositions 1–3), and consistent with set-wise supervenience, as the premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures show (Propositions 4–5; Table 4). The group's judgment on a conclusion can be fixed by members' judgments on premises alone. Emergent agency without members' conception of the group is judged unintelligible (§6). | Read |
| [NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md) | List — Three kinds of collective attitudes | Aggregate attitudes: a rule or market summarises members' attitudes; proposition-wise supervenience; no direct role; rationality contingent (majority beliefs on p, q, p∧q can be inconsistent, Table 1). Common attitudes: all hold, with common awareness; enriched proposition-wise supervenience; coordination; consistent by unanimity. Corporate attitudes: a group agent's; holistic supervenience, like non-reductive physicalism; action-guiding; rationality presupposed. Three lessons of near-independence; Table 2 summarises. | Read |
| [NOTE-568](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-568.md) | The Corporation as a Moral Person | A moral person is a non-eliminable subject of accountability, and that requires intentional agency. A corporation's Internal Decision (CID) Structure, an organizational chart plus recognition rules embedded in corporate policy, licenses redescribing members' acts as corporate acts done for corporate reasons. Corporations therefore differ in kind from mobs and can be full moral persons. That intentional agency suffices for moral personhood is asserted here and argued elsewhere. | Read |
| [NOTE-569](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-569.md) | The Conversable, Responsible Corporation | A syllogism. Corporations are conversable agents: through authorised spokespersons they avow attitudes and make commitments, and because mechanical aggregation can be inconsistent they must form minds of their own. Conversable agents are fit to be held responsible, having a significant choice, the capacity for normative judgment, and control over acting on it. So corporations are fit to be held responsible. | Read |
| [NOTE-575](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-575.md) | Précis of Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | The authors' own summary of Responsibility and Control. Moral responsibility requires guidance control, the agent's ownership of the mechanism that actually issues in action plus that mechanism's moderate reasons-responsiveness. Ownership comes from taking responsibility, a historical matter of dispositional self-beliefs acquired in appropriate ways. The result is compatible with causal determinism. | Read |
| [NOTE-579](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-579.md) | Responsiveness and Moral Responsibility | Fischer's first statement of reasons-responsiveness. Frankfurt-type cases show an agent can be responsible though he could not have done otherwise, so what must respond to reasons is the mechanism that actually issues in the action, not the agent. Weak responsiveness suffices: the actual kind of mechanism would do otherwise in some world with sufficient reason to. The result is semicompatibilism. | Read |
| [NOTE-582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-582.md) | Episteme Symposium on Group Agency: Replies to Gaus, Cariani, Sylvan, and Briggs | The authors answer four commentators on Group Agency. To Gaus: rationality is classical, ecological rationality is its relativisation to an environment, and robust group rationality may be relaxed without rescuing proposition-wise aggregation. To Cariani: chapter 4 offers possibility results. To Sylvan: group attitudes are not reducible to role-based member acceptance. To Briggs: group agents are fit to be held responsible in their own right, with rights restricted by normative individualism. | Read |
| [NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Argues that large models are a cultural and social technology, not intelligent agents: lossy, uninvertible summaries of human-produced corpora that, like prices and bureaucratic categories, allow the information to be reorganized at scale. The argument is by analogy and classification; no evidence is offered that could have come out otherwise. It names one mechanism (fitting the training distribution on average makes models worst where data are rare, which may homogenize culture) and leaves both it and its remedy untested. | Read |
